title: Nuclear and particle physics: practice questions (AI-written)

questions.question: A radioactive source has a half-life of 6.0 hours. The initial activity of the source is 480 Bq. Ignoring background radiation, what is the activity after 24 hours? A 20 Bq, B 30 Bq, C 60 Bq, D 120 Bq
questions.answer: B: 30 Bq
steps: 24 hours is 24 / 6.0 = 4 half-lives, so the activity is halved four times.
A divides by 24 (treats the decay as linear), C allows for only 3 half-lives, and D for only 2.

questions.question: A radioactive isotope has a decay constant of 0.035 s^-1. What is the half-life of the isotope? A 20 s, B 14 s, C 29 s, D 0.024 s
questions.answer: A: 20 s
steps: The half-life and decay constant are related by T1/2 = ln 2 / lambda.
T1/2 = 0.693 / 0.035 = 19.8 s, which is 20 s to 2 s.f. (option A).
B uses 0.5 / lambda, C uses 1 / lambda (the mean life), and D multiplies by ln 2 instead of dividing.

questions.question: A source of alpha particles is much more hazardous if it is swallowed than if it is held outside the body. Explain why.
questions.answer: Strongly ionising and short range: stopped by air or skin outside the body, but inside they damage living tissue.
steps: Alpha particles are strongly ionising: they transfer all their energy to the material within a very short distance
Outside the body they are absorbed by a few centimetres of air or by the dead outer layer of skin, so little reaches living tissue
Inside the body the source is in direct contact with living cells, so all the energy is absorbed in a small volume of tissue, damaging cells (DNA)
accept: Alpha particles have a range of only a few centimetres in air
Alpha particles are stopped by a sheet of paper
Damage to DNA can cause mutations or cancer
Beta and gamma radiation are less ionising, so they deposit less energy in a small volume

questions.question: A Geiger-Muller counter records 640 counts in 2.0 minutes when a source of gamma radiation is placed in front of it. With the source removed, the counter records 45 counts in 1.0 minute. Calculate the corrected count rate due to the source, in counts per second.
questions.answer: Corrected count rate = 4.6 counts s^-1.
steps: Count rate with the source = 640 / (2.0 x 60) = 5.333 counts s^-1.
Background count rate = 45 / 60 = 0.750 counts s^-1.
Corrected count rate = 5.333 - 0.750 = 4.58 counts s^-1, which is 4.6 counts s^-1 to 2 s.f.

questions.question: The mass of a helium-4 nucleus is 4.00151 u. The mass of a proton is 1.00728 u and the mass of a neutron is 1.00867 u. (1 u = 1.661 x 10^-27 kg.) Calculate the binding energy per nucleon of helium-4, in MeV.
questions.answer: Binding energy per nucleon = 7.1 MeV (total binding energy 28.4 MeV).
steps: Mass of separate nucleons = 2 x 1.00728 + 2 x 1.00867 = 4.03190 u.
Binding energy = (delta m) c^2 = 5.05 x 10^-29 x (3.00 x 10^8)^2 = 4.54 x 10^-12 J = 28.4 MeV (dividing by 1.60 x 10^-19 J per eV).
Binding energy per nucleon = 28.4 / 4 = 7.10 MeV, which is 7.1 MeV to 2 s.f.

questions.question: The isotope technetium-99m is used as a medical tracer. It emits gamma radiation only and has a half-life of 6.0 hours. State what is meant by the half-life of a radioactive isotope.
questions.answer: The time taken for the activity (or the number of undecayed nuclei) of a sample to fall to half of its initial value.
steps: The time taken for the number of undecayed nuclei (or the activity) of a sample to fall to half of its initial value
accept: The time for half of the unstable nuclei in a sample to decay
The time for the count rate (corrected for background) to halve
The average time for half of a large number of nuclei to decay, since decay is random

questions.question: A patient is injected with a sample of technetium-99m (half-life 6.0 hours) with an initial activity of 400 MBq. Calculate the activity of the sample 15 hours after the injection, assuming none has left the body.
questions.answer: Activity = 71 MBq.
steps: Number of half-lives = 15 / 6.0 = 2.5.
A = 70.7 MBq, about 71 MBq.

questions.question: The technetium-99m sample has an initial activity of 400 MBq and the half-life of technetium-99m is 6.0 hours. Calculate the number of technetium-99m nuclei in the sample when its activity is 400 MBq.
questions.answer: N = 1.2 x 10^13 nuclei (1.25 x 10^13 to 3 s.f.; decay constant 3.21 x 10^-5 s^-1).
steps: Decay constant lambda = ln 2 / T = 3.21 x 10^-5 s^-1.
Activity A = lambda N, so N = A / lambda = 4.00 x 10^8 / 3.21 x 10^-5 = 1.25 x 10^13 nuclei.

questions.question: Technetium-99m emits gamma radiation only and has a half-life of 6.0 hours. Evaluate its suitability as a tracer injected into the body, compared with an alpha-emitting isotope of half-life 100 years.
questions.answer: Suitable: gamma leaves the body and is weakly ionising, and the short half-life keeps the dose low; a 100-year alpha emitter is not.
steps: Gamma radiation is penetrating, so it leaves the body and can be detected outside, whereas alpha radiation would be absorbed in the tissue
Gamma radiation is weakly ionising, so it causes much less damage to cells than alpha particles absorbed inside the body
A half-life of 6 hours is long enough to complete the scan, but the activity falls to a very small value within a day or two, so the total dose is small
An isotope with a half-life of 100 years would remain active in the body for the rest of the patient's life, giving a continuing dose
accept: Gamma emission only means no alpha or beta particles are absorbed in the body, so the dose to the patient is lower
The short half-life means the tracer has decayed to a negligible activity before it can build up in the body or the environment
A short half-life gives a high activity from a small number of nuclei, so a small amount of tracer gives a detectable signal
A source with a half-life of 100 years has a very low activity from a given number of nuclei, so would need a large amount of material

questions.question: A K^+ meson is made of an up quark and an anti-strange quark. An up quark has charge +2/3 e and a strange quark has charge -1/3 e. What are the charge and the baryon number of the K^+ meson? A charge +1/3 e and baryon number 0, B charge +1/3 e and baryon number +2/3, C charge +1 e and baryon number +2/3, D charge +1 e and baryon number 0
questions.answer: D: charge +1 e and baryon number 0
steps: The anti-strange quark has charge +1/3 e, so the charge of the meson is +2/3 + 1/3 = +1 e.
Each quark has baryon number +1/3 and each antiquark -1/3, so the baryon number is +1/3 - 1/3 = 0, as for all mesons. This is option D.
A and B use the strange quark charge -1/3 e instead of that of the anti-strange quark; B and C add the baryon numbers of the quark and antiquark instead of subtracting.

questions.question: Which of the following decays obeys the conservation of charge, baryon number and lepton number? A p -> n + e+, B n -> p + e- + anti-electron-neutrino, C n -> p + e-, D p -> n + e+ + anti-electron-neutrino
questions.answer: B: n -> p + e- + anti-electron-neutrino
steps: Lepton numbers: electron +1, positron -1, electron-neutrino +1, anti-electron-neutrino -1. Nucleons have lepton number 0.
B: charge 0 -> +1 - 1 = 0; baryon number 1 -> 1; lepton number 0 -> +1 - 1 = 0. All three are conserved.
A has lepton number 0 -> -1, C has 0 -> +1, and D has 0 -> -1 - 1 = -2, so lepton number is not conserved in A, C and D.

questions.question: Protons are accelerated from rest at the centre of a cyclotron until they leave at the maximum radius of the dees. The magnetic flux density is unchanged but the alternating potential difference across the gap between the dees is doubled. Which row describes the kinetic energy of the protons when they leave and the number of revolutions they make? A kinetic energy doubles and number of revolutions halves, B kinetic energy doubles and number of revolutions unchanged, C kinetic energy unchanged and number of revolutions halves, D kinetic energy unchanged and number of revolutions doubles
questions.answer: C: kinetic energy unchanged and number of revolutions halves
steps: At the maximum radius R the speed is fixed by B q v = m v^2 / R, so v = B q R / m and the final kinetic energy q^2 B^2 R^2 / (2m) does not depend on the p.d.
In each revolution the protons cross the gap twice and gain 2qV, so the number of revolutions = final kinetic energy / (2qV).
Doubling V halves the number of revolutions: option C. A and B wrongly make the final energy depend on V; D inverts the effect on the number of revolutions.

questions.question: An up quark has charge +2/3 e and a down quark has charge -1/3 e. State the quark composition of a neutron and of an antiproton, and show that the antiproton has a charge of -e.
questions.answer: Neutron: up, down, down (udd). Antiproton: anti-up, anti-up, anti-down. Charge = -2/3 - 2/3 + 1/3 = -1 e.
steps: Neutron: one up quark and two down quarks (u d d)
Antiproton: two anti-up quarks and one anti-down quark
Charge of antiproton = -2/3 - 2/3 + 1/3 = -1 e
accept: The antiproton is made of the antiparticles of the quarks in a proton (u u d)
Neutron charge check: +2/3 - 1/3 - 1/3 = 0
Anti-up has charge -2/3 e and anti-down has charge +1/3 e

questions.question: A gamma-ray photon passes close to a nucleus and produces an electron-positron pair. Calculate the minimum energy of the photon, in MeV, and the corresponding minimum frequency.
questions.answer: Minimum energy = 1.02 MeV (1.64 x 10^-13 J); minimum frequency = 2.47 x 10^20 Hz.
steps: The minimum photon energy equals the rest energy of the two particles, which have equal masses: E = 2 m_e c^2.

questions.question: A proton moves at 4.5 x 10^6 m s^-1 in a circular path in a uniform magnetic field of flux density 0.80 T, perpendicular to the field. Calculate (i) the radius of the path and (ii) the frequency of the alternating potential difference that would accelerate the proton in a cyclotron with this field.
steps: (i) The magnetic force provides the centripetal force: B q v = m v^2 / r, so r = m v / (B q).
(ii) The frequency of revolution is f = v / (2 pi r) = B q / (2 pi m), which does not depend on speed.

questions.question: Charged particles produced in a collision leave tracks in a detector that is in a uniform magnetic field perpendicular to the tracks. Explain how the tracks can be used to deduce the sign of the charge on a particle and its momentum.
questions.answer: The direction in which the track curves gives the sign of the charge (force direction from F = Bqv); the radius r gives the momentum, p = B q r.
steps: The magnetic force on a moving charge is perpendicular to its velocity, so the particle follows a circular arc
The direction of curvature, with the field direction and the particle motion (Fleming's left-hand rule), shows whether the charge is positive or negative
From B q v = m v^2 / r the momentum is p = m v = B q r, so a larger radius means a larger momentum for the same charge
A track that spirals inwards shows the particle is losing energy (by ionisation), so its momentum decreases
accept: Oppositely charged particles curve in opposite directions in the same field
The radius of curvature is proportional to momentum for a given charge and field strength
A particle that leaves no track and is not deflected is uncharged
Charge can be compared from track curvature if the momenta are equal (r = p / Bq)

questions.question: A positron is the antiparticle of the electron. State two properties of a positron that are different from those of an electron.
questions.answer: A positron has charge +e (the electron has -e) and lepton number -1 (the electron has +1).
steps: Charge: the positron has charge +e (+1.60 x 10^-19 C) but the electron has -e
Lepton number: the positron has -1 but the electron has +1
accept: Deflected in the opposite direction to an electron in the same electric or magnetic field (a consequence of the opposite charge)
The positron is the antiparticle (antimatter) whereas the electron is an ordinary matter particle
An antilepton rather than a lepton

questions.question: A slow-moving electron and a slow-moving positron annihilate to produce two gamma-ray photons. Explain why two photons, rather than one, are produced and why they travel in opposite directions.
questions.answer: Total momentum is about zero, which needs two photons with equal and opposite momenta.
steps: Momentum must be conserved; before the annihilation the total momentum is approximately zero
A single photon always has momentum (h / lambda), so one photon would leave a non-zero total momentum
Two photons with equal magnitudes of momentum (equal energies) travelling in opposite directions have a total momentum of zero
accept: Energy is conserved: the total energy of the two photons equals the rest energy of the pair
Charge, lepton number and baryon number are all zero before and after
The photons have equal wavelengths and frequencies since they have equal energies

questions.question: An electron and a positron, both at rest, annihilate to produce two photons of equal energy. Calculate the wavelength of each photon.
questions.answer: Wavelength = 2.4 x 10^-12 m.
steps: Each photon has energy equal to the rest energy of one particle: E = m_e c^2 = 9.11 x 10^-31 x (3.00 x 10^8)^2 = 8.20 x 10^-14 J.
E = h c / lambda, so lambda = h c / E.

questions.question: In another annihilation the electron and the positron each have a kinetic energy of 0.30 MeV just before they meet, and the two photons have equal energies. Calculate the wavelength of each photon and compare it with your answer to (c).
questions.answer: Wavelength = 1.5 x 10^-12 m, shorter than in (c) because the photons carry the kinetic energy as well.
steps: Energy of each photon = rest energy + kinetic energy of one particle = 0.511 + 0.30 = 0.81 MeV (1.30 x 10^-13 J, using 9.11 x 10^-31 x (3.00 x 10^8)^2 as the rest energy).
This is shorter than the 2.4 x 10^-12 m in (c), because the photons have more energy.

questions.question: An alpha particle of kinetic energy E is fired directly at a stationary nucleus and comes momentarily to rest at a distance d from the nucleus. A second alpha particle of kinetic energy 2E is fired directly at the same nucleus. What is its distance of closest approach? A d / 4, B d / 2, C d / sqrt(2), D 2d
questions.answer: B: d / 2
steps: At the closest approach all the kinetic energy has become electric potential energy: E = Q q / (4 pi epsilon0 d), so d is proportional to 1 / E.
Doubling the kinetic energy halves the distance of closest approach: d / 2, option B.
A takes d proportional to 1 / E^2, C takes it proportional to 1 / sqrt(E) (as if from the speed), and D takes it proportional to E.

questions.question: An electron in a hydrogen atom moves from the energy level at -0.85 eV to the energy level at -3.40 eV. Which row describes the photon involved? A absorbed with energy 2.55 eV, B absorbed with energy 4.25 eV, C emitted with energy 2.55 eV, D emitted with energy 4.25 eV
questions.answer: C: emitted with energy 2.55 eV
steps: The electron moves to a lower (more negative) energy level, so the atom loses energy and a photon is emitted.
The photon energy = -0.85 - (-3.40) = 2.55 eV, option C.
A and B describe absorption, which needs a move to a higher level. B and D add the two energies (0.85 + 3.40 = 4.25 eV) instead of subtracting.

questions.question: In Rutherford's experiment, most alpha particles passed through a thin gold foil with little or no deflection, but about 1 in 8000 was deflected through more than 90 degrees. Explain what these two observations show about the structure of the atom.
questions.answer: Most of the atom is empty space, and the positive charge and most of the mass are concentrated in a very small, dense nucleus.
steps: Most alpha particles pass straight through, so most of the atom is empty space
A few are deflected through large angles, so they meet a strong repulsive force from a concentrated region of positive charge (the nucleus)

Only about 1 in 8000 is deflected through a large angle, so the nucleus is very small compared with the atom, and it contains most of the mass because it can reverse the motion of the massive alpha particle
accept: The charge is not spread through the atom, which rules out the plum pudding model
The deflected alpha particles are repelled, so the nucleus has the same sign of charge as the alpha particles (positive)
Alpha particles that pass closest to a nucleus are deflected through the largest angles

questions.question: An alpha particle of kinetic energy 4.8 MeV is fired directly at a stationary silver nucleus (proton number 47). Treat both as point charges and assume the nucleus remains at rest. Calculate the distance of closest approach and state what this shows about the radius of a silver nucleus.
questions.answer: Closest approach = 2.8 x 10^-14 m; the radius of the silver nucleus must be smaller than this.
steps: At closest approach all the kinetic energy has become electric potential energy: KE = Q q / (4 pi epsilon0 r).
The alpha particle has not touched the nucleus (it was repelled by the Coulomb force), so the nuclear radius is less than about 2.8 x 10^-14 m.

questions.question: Electrons with an energy of 250 MeV are used to investigate the structure of nuclei. For electrons of this energy the momentum p is given by E = pc. Calculate the de Broglie wavelength of the electrons and explain why electrons of such a high energy are needed to investigate the size of a nucleus.
questions.answer: Wavelength = 5.0 x 10^-15 m; the wavelength must be comparable to or smaller than the nuclear size (about 10^-15 m) for diffraction and detail to be observed.
steps: p = E / c and lambda = h / p = h c / E.
Significant diffraction (and a pattern that reveals structure) occurs only when the wavelength is comparable to the size of the object, and nuclei have diameters of the order of 10^-15 m.
A shorter de Broglie wavelength needs a larger momentum, so high-energy electrons are needed.

questions.question: The energy levels of a hydrogen atom are -13.6 eV, -3.40 eV, -1.51 eV and -0.85 eV for the first four levels (n = 1 to 4), with zero energy for a free electron at rest. State what is meant by the ionisation energy of a hydrogen atom.
questions.answer: The minimum energy needed to remove the electron from a hydrogen atom in its ground state (13.6 eV).
steps: The minimum energy needed to remove an electron from an atom in its ground state (13.6 eV for hydrogen)
accept: The energy needed to raise the electron from the ground-state level (-13.6 eV) to the zero energy level (0 eV)
The energy needed to move the electron from n = 1 to infinity

questions.question: Calculate the minimum frequency of a photon that can ionise a hydrogen atom in its ground state (ionisation energy 13.6 eV).
steps: E = h f, so f = E / h.

questions.question: A free electron of kinetic energy 12.5 eV collides with a hydrogen atom in its ground state. The first four energy levels are -13.6 eV, -3.40 eV, -1.51 eV and -0.85 eV. Deduce to which of these levels the atom could be excited by the collision.
questions.answer: The atom could be excited to n = 2 (needs 10.2 eV) or n = 3 (needs 12.1 eV), but not to n = 4 (needs 12.75 eV, which is more than 12.5 eV).
steps: Energy needed from n = 1 to n = 2: 13.6 - 3.40 = 10.2 eV (less than 12.5 eV, so possible).
Energy needed from n = 1 to n = 3: 13.6 - 1.51 = 12.09 eV (less than 12.5 eV, so possible).
Energy needed from n = 1 to n = 4: 13.6 - 0.85 = 12.75 eV, more than 12.5 eV, so not possible.

questions.question: Some hydrogen atoms are excited to the n = 3 level and then return to the ground state, emitting photons. State the number of different photon energies that can be emitted.
questions.answer: Three (n = 3 to n = 1, n = 3 to n = 2 and n = 2 to n = 1).
steps: Three (transitions 3 to 1, 3 to 2 and 2 to 1, each with a different energy change)
accept: Three spectral lines, from n = 3 to 1, n = 3 to 2 and n = 2 to 1
Three different wavelengths (or frequencies) of radiation

questions.question: Calculate the longest wavelength of the photons emitted when atoms in the n = 3 level (-1.51 eV) return to lower levels. The n = 2 level is at -3.40 eV.
questions.answer: Longest wavelength = 6.6 x 10^-7 m (about 660 nm, red light), from the n = 3 to n = 2 transition.
steps: The longest wavelength corresponds to the smallest photon energy, which is the transition from n = 3 to n = 2.
